Validation and leakage

Source: vignettes/articles/validation-and-leakage.Rmd
validation-and-leakage.Rmd

Feature selection is easy to get wrong in a way that makes results look better than they are. The usual cause is that the rows used to choose the features are also used to judge them. This article shows the problem on data where the right answer is known, lists which numbers featR reports are honest and which are optimistic, and walks through a pipeline that keeps them apart.

The rule

Anything that looks at the outcome is part of model fitting. That covers choosing features, tuning, and any imputation or scaling learned from the data. If rows that will later measure performance took part in any of those steps, the measurement is optimistic. The classic case is selecting features on the full data and then cross-validating a model on those features. On pure noise it reports a fit where there is none.

Selection bias, demonstrated

Here the outcome is pure noise. No feature predicts it, so an honest estimate of out-of-sample R² should be at or below zero. The code picks the 10 predictors most correlated with y using fs_supervised(), fits lm() on them, and scores it by 5-fold cross-validation, once with the selection outside the folds and once inside.

set.seed(42)
n <- 60; p <- 500
X <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p))
X$y <- rnorm(n)

folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n))

cv_r2 <- function(select_inside) {
  pred <- numeric(n)
  if (!select_inside) {
    # WRONG: choose the 10 "best" features using all rows, including every
    # future test fold
    keep <- names(sort(fs_supervised(X, "y")$scores, decreasing = TRUE))[1:10]
  }
  for (k in 1:5) {
    train <- X[folds != k, ]
    test  <- X[folds == k, ]
    if (select_inside) {
      # RIGHT: choose features using the training fold only
      keep <- names(sort(fs_supervised(train, "y")$scores,
                         decreasing = TRUE))[1:10]
    }
    fit <- lm(y ~ ., data = train[, c(keep, "y")])
    pred[folds == k] <- predict(fit, test)
  }
  1 - sum((X$y - pred)^2) / sum((X$y - mean(X$y))^2)
}

c(selection_outside_cv = cv_r2(FALSE), selection_inside_cv = cv_r2(TRUE))
#> selection_outside_cv  selection_inside_cv 
#>            0.4496028           -0.8262182

With the selection outside the loop, cross-validation reports an R² of 0.45 for a model of noise. With the selection inside the loop, R² is -0.83. Nothing predicts y, and a model of 10 noise predictors fitted on 48 rows predicts worse than the mean, so a negative R² is what an honest estimate should show. Ambroise and McLachlan (2002) describe this selection bias. It applies to every method in featR, including the cheap filters.

What featR does for you

Where a featR function reports a performance number, it tries to make that number honest, and where it cannot, the documentation says so.

  • fs_randomforest(), fs_mars(), fs_recursivefeature(), and fs_svm() split the data into training and test rows first. Selection, tuning, and any preprocessing that learns from the data (near-zero-variance filters, correlation filters, one-hot encoders, imputation values) are fitted on the training rows only, so their test-set metrics come from rows the selection never saw. The exception is fs_randomforest()’s control$preprocess hook, which runs on the full data before the split.
  • fs_svm() repeats SVM-RFE inside every cross-validation fold when it chooses how many features to keep. fs_elastic(use_pca = TRUE) refits the centering, scaling, and PCA inside every resample. Class upsampling in fs_mars() and fs_svm() also happens inside each resample, so a duplicated row never appears on both sides of a fold.
  • fs_lasso() refuses missing predictors by default instead of imputing them from the full data. If you opt in with impute = "mean", it uses full-data means and warns that this leaks.
  • Numbers computed on the rows used for selection are documented as optimistic. The table below lists them.
  • Known false-positive behavior is documented too. fs_boruta() can confirm pure-noise features, especially with resolve_tentative = TRUE, which settles undecided features with Boruta::TentativeRoughFix(); the wrapper methods guide shows a real case.

Which reported numbers are honest

A number is honest here if it was computed on rows that took no part in choosing the features or the tuning values. Anything else is optimistic and will, on average, flatter the model.

Function Honest (held-out) Optimistic or in-sample
fs_unsupervised(), fs_correlation(), fs_pca(), fs_svd() No performance number. They never look at an outcome. None from the function.
fs_supervised(), fs_infogain() No performance number. scores describe the rows you passed. Any model then scored on those rows is optimistic.
fs_chi() No performance number. scores are adjusted p-values of one test per feature. They are marginal tests, not a model’s performance, and a model built on the significant features and scored on the same rows is optimistic.
fs_lasso() None. No rows are held out. The cross-validated error curve in model$cvm (with return_model = TRUE). Its value at lambda.min is the minimum over the whole lambda path.
fs_elastic() None. No rows are held out. details$metric_value (the best value over the whole alpha/lambda grid) and model$results.
fs_randomforest() details$metrics details$oob when a control$feature_select hook looked at the target. Anything learned in control$preprocess, which runs before the split, also flatters details$metrics.
fs_mars() details$metrics model$results and model$resample: tuning cross-validation on the training rows, and the best row over the grid.
fs_recursivefeature() details$test_metrics details$resampling_results, and model$results when return_final_model = TRUE.
fs_svm() details$performance The chosen size’s entry in details$selection$size_scores (the best of up to six estimates), and model$results and model$resample when feature_select = TRUE.
fs_boruta() No performance number. details$decisions can confirm noise features. In the simulation described in ?fs_boruta (one real and three noise predictors, 150 rows), Boruta confirmed 5 percent of the noise predictors, and 8.3 percent with resolve_tentative = TRUE.
fs_stepwise() None. scores (absolute t statistics), the p-values in details$coefficients, and anything from summary(model).
fs_bayes() None. details$mae and details$rmse (in-sample), details$best_elpd and details$loo_comparison (the winner of the search), and the posterior of the returned model.

The held-out metrics also follow different conventions across functions. fs_mars(), fs_recursivefeature(), and fs_svm() report caret’s R², which is the squared correlation between predictions and observations. It is never negative and ignores bias, so predictions of 2 * y score 1. fs_randomforest() reports 1 - SSE/SST on the test rows, which can be negative. For binary classification, fs_randomforest() treats the second factor level as the positive class by default and fs_mars() the first. ROC AUC does not depend on that choice, but sensitivity and PR AUC do.

Every held-out number above comes from one train/test split, so on small data it is noisy. A held-out split protects the metrics of that one call, not your workflow.

What you still have to do

If you try five methods, look at their test metrics, and keep the best one, the test set has become part of selection. The remedy:

  1. Split off a final test set once, before anything looks at the outcome.
  2. Do all exploration, method comparison, and tuning on the remaining rows. Where you cross-validate, repeat the selection inside every fold, as in the demonstration above.
  3. Use the test set once, at the end, to report the pipeline you chose.

A worked pipeline

The data have 20 independent standard-normal predictors plus X21, a near-copy of X1. The outcome depends on X1, X2, and X3 with noise standard deviation 1.

set.seed(7)
n <- 300
d <- data.frame(matrix(rnorm(n * 20), n, 20))
d$X21 <- d$X1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.05)                  # near-duplicate of X1
d$y <- 1.5 * d$X1 - 1 * d$X2 + 0.5 * d$X3 + rnorm(n)

# 1. Split once
test_rows <- sample(n, 75)
train <- d[-test_rows, ]
test  <- d[test_rows, ]

# 2. Outcome-free cleaning, then redundancy pruning, on training rows only
predictors <- setdiff(names(train), "y")
dedup <- fs_correlation(train[, predictors], threshold = 0.95)
dedup$details$dropped
#> [1] "X1"

# 3. Model-based selection on training rows only
sel <- fs_lasso(train[, c(selected(dedup), "y")], "y", nfolds = 5, seed = 1)
selected(sel)
#> [1] "X21" "X2"  "X3"  "X20" "X19" "X11" "X18"

# 4. Refit and evaluate once on the untouched test rows
fit <- lm(reformulate(selected(sel), "y"), data = train)
pred <- predict(fit, test)
c(test_RMSE = sqrt(mean((test$y - pred)^2)))
#> test_RMSE 
#>  1.159347

fs_correlation() does not look at the outcome, so it may keep either member of the X1/X21 pair. Here it dropped X1 and kept X21, which carries the same information. Lasso then kept X21, X2, and X3 plus four noise predictors, because lambda.min optimizes prediction rather than recovery of the true predictors; lambda = "1se" gives a sparser choice. The noise standard deviation is 1, so no model can do much better than a test RMSE of 1. This pipeline’s 1.16 is an honest estimate from 75 rows that took no part in any step.

Post-selection inference

The p-values, confidence intervals, and posterior intervals of a model whose predictors were chosen on the same data are not valid in the usual sense. They are too small, too narrow, or too confident. That applies to summary(fs_stepwise(...)$model) and to the posterior of the model fs_bayes() returns. Treat them as descriptive. For valid inference, select on one part of the data and estimate on another (sample splitting), or use a dedicated selective-inference method.

Reference

Ambroise, C. and McLachlan, G. J. (2002). Selection bias in gene extraction on the basis of microarray gene-expression data. PNAS 99(10), 6562–6566. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.102102699
